Third, focusing solely on the Duke memorandum, the Court held that its 
rationale for DACA rescission was arbitrary and capricious. Specifically, the 
Court concluded that Duke “did not appear to appreciate the full scope of her 
discretion,” which authorized her to pick among alternatives after the Attorney 
General’s determination that DACA was illegal. Specifically, the Attorney 
General had relied on the Fifth Circuit’s opinion in Texas v. United States, 
which in turn “described the ‘core’ issue before it as the ‘Secretary’s decision’ 
to grant ‘eligibility for benefits’—including work authorization. Social Security, 
and Medicare—^to unauthorized aliens on ‘a class-wide basis.’ ” But as the 
Court pointed out, there is “more to DAPA (and DACA) than such benefits,” 
including “[t]he defining feature of deferred action * * * the decision to defer 
removal (and to notify the affected alien of that decision.’ ” According to the 
Court, the Fifth Circuit in Texas “was careful to distinguish that forbearance 
component from eligibility for benefits.” Thus, the Court noted that “removing 
benefits eligibility while continuing forbearance remained squarely within the 
discretion of Acting Secretary Duke,” but Duke’s memorandum “offer[ed] no 
reason for terminating forbearance,” instead “treat[ing] the Attorney General’s 
conclusion regarding the illegality of benefits as sufficient to rescind both 
benefits and forbearance, without explanation.” The Court explained that 
Duke’s “reasoning repeated the error we identified in one of our leading modern 
administrative law cases,” State Farm, The DACA memorandum “could not be 
rescinded in full ‘without any consideration whatsoever’ of a forbearance-only 
policy.” State Farm, the Court concluded, “teaches that when an agency 
rescinds a prior pohcy its reasoned analysis must consider the ‘alternative[s]’ 
that are ‘within the ambit of the existing [policy].’ ”
The Court also identified a second failure to address a relevant topic: 
“whether there was ‘legitimate reliance’ on the DACA memorandum.” Relying 
on Fox, the Court said that “[wjhen an agency changes course, as DHS did here, 
it must ‘be cognizant that longstanding policies may have ‘engendered serious 
reliance interests that must be taken into account.’ ” The Court rejected the 
notion that DACA recipients lacked a legally cognizable reliance interest 
because the original DACA memorandum itself stated that the program 
“conferred no substantive rights.” Such disclaimers, the Court said, “are surely 
pertinent to considering the strength of any reliance interests, but that 
consideration must be undertaken by the agency in the first instance.” To be 
sure, the Court observed, the agency could reject the strength of any rehance 
interests, but “[mjaking that difficult decision was the agency’s job,” which the 
agency failed to do.
Justice Thomas dissented. He claimed that “the Trump administration 
rescinded DACA the same way that the Obama administrated created it: 
unilaterally, and through a mere memorandum.” According to Justice Thomas, 
the agency’s decision to rescind an unlawful program is “clearly reasonable,” 
“[s]o long as the agency’s determination of illegality is sound.” Because of the 
majority opinion. Justice Thomas contended, “a dministrations can bind their
